newsitem.title: INDIA: India steelmakers hope demand will offset duty cut.
newsitem.headline: India steelmakers hope demand will offset duty cut.

text.p: India's steelmakers, already struggling with sluggish demand, have been hit by a cut in the import tariff on cold rolled coils, but an increase in demand could soften the blow, officials and analysts said on Tuesday.
"The domestic industry will suffer because of the cut in duty on cold rolled coils," V. Raghuraman, secretary general of the Associated Chambers of Commerce and Industry (Assocham) told Reuters.

Finance Minister P. Chidambaram in his 1997/98 (April-March) federal budget last Friday singled out cold rolled steel coils for a cut in import duty to 25 percent from 30 percent to help the country's engineering industry.
CR coils are mainly used in cars, refrigerators, and furniture.
India produced 21.4 million tonnes of finished steel in 1995/96 (April-March). During the year it imported about two million tonnes of steel, mainly hot rolled and cold rolled coils and semis.
Analysts said at the end of November 1996, steel companies held nearly 1.5 million tonnes of unsold steel stocks.
"The CR coils reduction will hit Steel Authority of India Ltd (SAIL) the most," said Sanjay Jain of broking firm James Capel B & K. "The overall aim of the budget is to boost demand."
"The cost of production will come down but demand is important since inventories were piling up," said Raghuraman.
Jain said the finance minister had tried to soften the effect of input costs to mollify SAIL.
Chidambaram reduced import duties on several raw materials for the steel industry including coking coal, coke, nickel, ferro-alloys and re-rollable steel scrap, to cut production costs.
Raghuraman said Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) countries were dumping CR coils and the government must strictly enforce laws on dumping to protect the domestic industry.
"If the anti-dumping duties are strictly imposed, the distress will be less," he said.

Analysts said rising input costs, stagnation in demand from the construction, automobile and white goods segments, a drastic fall in the prices of coils in the world market and a continuing liquidity crunch were severely affecting steel producers.

They said the cumulative impact of increases in prices of inputs in 1996/97 (April-March) would have an adverse impact on steelmakers like state-owned SAIL and private-sector Tata Iron and Steel Co (TISCO) and Lloyd Steel.
In 1996/97 the government raised coking coal prices by 27 percent, petroleum products prices went up between 15 and 25 percent and railway freight was hiked by 10 percent.

"In the present difficult market for steel, it is interesting to note that the import duty (for steel items) has not been changed. However, in the case of cold rolled materials, there would be some adverse effect," SAIL chairman Arvind Pande said in a statement.
He said the concessions on import of coking coal and nickel would help SAIL and the budget would stimulate industrial activity which the industry was looking forward to.
SAIL officials said the company had in urged finance minister Chidambaram to increase the customs duty on cold rolled coils and sheets to 35 percent from the existing 30 percent.
